newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Rotterdam street fest pays tribute to Marshall aid.
newsitem.headline: Rotterdam street fest pays tribute to Marshall aid.

text.p: Thousands of Dutch and Americans cheered U.S. President Bill Clinton in Rotterdam on Wednesday in a show of thanks for post-World War Two U.S. aid that helped rebuild the city 50 years ago into the world's biggest port.

The highlight of a street party on a clear evening in the futuristic Kop van Zuid neighbourhood was Clinton's unveiling of a brass plaque of George Marshall, the U.S. Secretary of State who initiated over $12 billion in aid to war-torn Europe in 1947 -- worth $88 billion in today's terms.
"Here in Europe, the Marshall Plan helped rebuild a continent ravaged by war, gave strength to fragile democracies and sparked unparalleled prosperity," Clinton said.

"Our purpose must be to summon the spirit of the Marshall generation to create a structure of opportunity, freedom and security for the next 50 years and beyond," he told a flag-waving crowd swelled by some 4,000 Americans now living in the Netherlands.
Dutch organisers of the celebrations laid on a fun fair at a Rotterdam quay from where more than a million Dutch people emigrated to America in the 1930s.

Clinton's audience, including members of the Dutch cabinet and royal family, was seated in the shadow of sea-containers and near the modern Erasmus Bridge, completed last year, a symbol of Rotterdam's most recent urban renewal.
A master of ceremonies introduced Rotterdam as "the most American of Dutch cities".

Accompanied by his wife Hillary, dressed in a coral suit and sporting sunglasses, a relaxed Clinton watched video footage of Rotterdam 50 years ago, a blitzed city with huge swathes of the centre reduced to rubble by German bombing raids.
Mary Fischer, among the many local Rotterdammers attending the festivities, caught the mood of celebration and gratitude.
"It's a 'thank you' to America," she told Reuters.
"I was seven when the Marshall Plan was instituted...I don't remember much of it myself but my father was an entrepreneur and he benefited."
"The Marshall Plan meant a major investment...I remember there were suddenly lots of great goods lorries piled high with things we hadn't seen for years," said Henk Roos, an elderly Rotterdammer.
"We didn't notice it immediately in terms of living standards, but later it began to work through," he said.
His wife Johanna added: "Immediately after the war the port was in ruins, the (occupying) Germans blew up everything before they left."
Around one tenth of the Marshall billions flowing into Europe five decades ago were channelled into the Netherlands, with Rotterdam one of the main beneficiaries.
"Rotterdam profited as did no other (Dutch) city from Marshall Aid," said a spokesman for the port authority.
"The dollars that went to aid the recovery of agriculture, trade and industry in the Netherlands and other western European countries meant the recovery of the Port of Rotterdam."

In providing Europe's devastated economies with much-needed cash for food, machinery, grain, raw materials and other goods, the Marshall Plan boosted trade flows through Rotterdam harbour back to pre-war levels.
Today's Rotterdam is a key transport hub, transshipping some 292 million tonnes of cargo annually.
